key_terms.meaning: Steady voltage across a cell membrane at rest, about −70 mV inside relative to outside, set mainly by K⁺ leak and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
Brief all-or-none reversal of membrane voltage to about +30 mV, then back, lasting 1–2 ms in nerve
The depolarisation level (about −55 mV) a stimulus must reach before an action potential fires
E = (RT/zF)·ln([ion]out/[ion]in), the equilibrium voltage for one ion species across the membrane
Fixed DC voltage an electrode metal develops against body electrolyte; differs between metals and adds an offset to the bio-signal
Charged layer of ions in the electrolyte that sits against the electrode surface and lets ionic current cross into electronic current
Complex opposition (resistance plus capacitance) at the electrode–skin interface, typically 1–10 kΩ for a good surface electrode
Electrode with a tip of 1 µm or less, used to record from a single cell without damaging it
Device that converts one form of energy (force, pressure, temperature, light) into an electrical output
Resistive element whose resistance changes with stretch; gauge factor G = (ΔR/R)/(ΔL/L)
Four-arm resistive network that converts a small resistance change into a measurable voltage; output V₀ = V·(ΔR/R)/4 for one active arm
Production of charge across certain crystals when stressed, used for pressure and vibration sensors
Three-op-amp difference amplifier with very high input impedance and high gain, the front end of every bio-amplifier
Common-mode rejection ratio, CMRR = 20·log₁₀(A<sub>d</sub>/A<sub>cm</sub>) in dB; tells how well the amplifier rejects the shared interference voltage
Model of the heart as a dipole viewed by leads I, II and III on the two arms and left leg, with lead II = lead I + lead III
NCV = d / (t₂ − t₁), where d is the distance between two stimulation points in metres and t₂ − t₁ is the difference in latency in seconds
Portable recorder that stores a continuous 24-hour ECG on the patient for later scanning and arrhythmia analysis
Small EEG response time-locked to a repeated stimulus (visual, auditory or somatosensory), recovered by averaging many trials
Training method in which a patient sees or hears a filtered EEG or EMG signal and learns to change it
Pressure-sensitive platform or insole that maps foot loading during standing and walking

takeaways: Every bioelectric signal starts as an ion movement across a membrane, so the source voltage is always a chemical battery of a few tens of millivolts.
An electrode is an ionic-to-electronic converter; its half-cell potential and its impedance decide how clean the recorded signal will be.
A transducer must be chosen by range, sensitivity, linearity, impedance and safety for the specific body variable, not by one single best type.
A bio-amplifier's job is to multiply the difference between two electrodes and throw away the interference both share, which is why CMRR and input impedance matter more than plain gain.
The ECG recorder is a calibrated voltmeter and clock: standard leads, 1 mV calibration pulse, 25 mm/s paper speed and 10 mm/mV sensitivity.
EEG needs microvolt gain in a 0.5–70 Hz band while EMG needs millivolt gain up to about 500 Hz; one amplifier setting cannot serve both.
Nerve conduction velocity turns two latency readings at two stimulation sites into a number in metres per second that separates normal nerve from demyelination.
Most ECG faults are found by checking, in order, the patient, the electrode, the cable and amplifier, and lastly the mains interference path.
Averaging and filtering pull evoked potentials out of background EEG because the response repeats while the noise does not.
Biofeedback works only when the measured signal is clean and the feedback reaches the patient within a fraction of a second.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are almost always asked as a signal path — physiology, then electrode, then amplifier, then recorder or display — so draw the block chain and give a number with units at every block.

bank.q: Explain the origin of the resting membrane potential and the action potential in a nerve cell, and state typical voltage and time values.
outline: Ion concentrations inside and outside the cell with typical millivolt values
K⁺ leak sets the resting voltage near −70 mV; Na⁺/K⁺ pump maintains gradients
Nernst and Goldman relations used to compute equilibrium voltages
Depolarisation to threshold near −55 mV opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Peak near +30 mV, repolarisation by K⁺ efflux, refractory period
All-or-none law and propagation along the axon

answer.text: Ion distribution. The membrane separates solutions of different make-up. Typical neuron values (mmol/L):

answer: Membrane and pump. The lipid membrane is an insulator about 5 nm thick, so it acts as a capacitor; ions cross only through channels. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per cycle. It keeps the gradients in the table and, because it moves one net charge out per cycle, adds a few millivolts of extra negativity.

Nernst equation. For one ion the equilibrium voltage is E = (61.5 mV ÷ z) log₁₀([out] ÷ [in]) at 37 °C. At E<sub>K</sub> = −89.1 mV the electric pull on K⁺ exactly balances its outward concentration push, so no net K⁺ moves.

answer.text: Origin of the resting potential (Goldman equation). At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺. With P<sub>K</sub> : P<sub>Na</sub> : P<sub>Cl</sub> = 1 : 0.04 : 0.45:

answer: So the resting potential, about −70 mV, lies close to E<sub>K</sub> but a little less negative, because a small Na⁺ leak carries positive charge in. The inside is negative because K⁺ leaves down its gradient and the large proteins that stay behind are negative.

head: Phase
What opens or closes
Typical value
rows: Na⁺ channels inactivate, K⁺ channels open
back to rest about 1–2 ms after onset
slow K⁺ channels still open, V<sub>m</sub> moves toward E<sub>K</sub>

answer: The peak (+30 mV) stays below E<sub>Na</sub> (+60.6 mV) because the Na⁺ channels inactivate and the K⁺ channels open before V<sub>m</sub> can reach the sodium equilibrium.

Refractory period and the all-or-none law. During the absolute refractory period (about 1 ms in nerve) no stimulus can fire the cell, because the Na⁺ channels are inactivated; during the relative refractory period only a stronger stimulus can. Once threshold is crossed the spike has a fixed size, so a stronger stimulus raises the firing rate, not the height. This also caps the firing rate near 1 ÷ 1 ms = 1000 spikes/s.

Propagation. Inward Na⁺ current at the active patch spreads along the axon and depolarises the next patch to threshold, so the spike travels without losing size. In myelinated fibres it jumps between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction) at roughly 50 m/s in large arm nerves, the value a nerve conduction study measures.

Closing check: depolarisation to threshold = (−55) − (−70) = 15 mV; spike amplitude = (+30) − (−70) = 100 mV; the Goldman value −67.3 mV lies between E<sub>K</sub> = −89.1 mV and E<sub>Na</sub> = +60.6 mV, as it must.

bank.q: Describe the electrode–electrolyte interface, half-cell potential and why electrode impedance must match the amplifier.
outline: Ionic current in tissue, electronic current in wire, conversion at the interface
Double layer model and its capacitance
Half-cell potential; offset from two different metals; need for Ag/AgCl pairs
Polarisation, non-polarisable electrodes, electrode jelly and skin preparation
Typical surface electrode impedance 1–10 kΩ; causes of drift and motion artefact
Why amplifier input impedance must be many times the electrode impedance
answer: Ionic to electronic current. In tissue and gel the current is carried by ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻); in the lead wire by electrons. At an Ag/AgCl electrode the reactions Ag ⇌ Ag⁺ + e⁻ and Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ ⇌ AgCl hand charge across the boundary.

Double layer. The reaction leaves a sheet of charge on the metal and an opposite sheet of ions in the electrolyte a fraction of a nanometre away. Two charge sheets that close together form a capacitance C<sub>d</sub>, and the charge-transfer path through the reaction is a resistance R<sub>d</sub> in parallel with it.

Half-cell potential. The double layer holds a steady voltage, measured against the standard hydrogen electrode; for Ag/AgCl it is about +0.22 V. Two identical electrodes give equal and opposite half-cell potentials, so only their small difference, a few millivolts, reaches the amplifier as offset. Two different metals can leave hundreds of millivolts, far more than a 1 mV ECG.

Polarisation. When current flows, the half-cell potential shifts (overpotential). A polarisable electrode such as bare stainless steel behaves like a capacitor and drifts; Ag/AgCl in chloride gel is almost non-polarisable because its reaction reverses easily, so the offset stays small and steady. Skin preparation and gel lower the skin resistance and reduce motion artefact.

answer.text: Equivalent circuit. Each electrode is E<sub>hc</sub> in series with R<sub>s</sub> (gel and skin) and the parallel pair R<sub>d</sub> ∥ C<sub>d</sub>. As frequency rises the reactance of C<sub>d</sub> falls, so impedance falls; a gelled surface electrode is about 1–10 kΩ in the ECG band, unprepared skin tens of kΩ or more.

Why the amplifier input impedance must be much larger. Electrode and input form a divider, V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>bio</sub> × Z<sub>in</sub> ÷ (Z<sub>in</sub> + Z<sub>e</sub>). For Z<sub>e</sub> = 50 kΩ:

Why the two electrodes must also match. Mains gives the body a common-mode voltage V<sub>cm</sub>. Each electrode divides it against the common-mode input impedance Z<sub>cm</sub>. Take V<sub>cm</sub> = 100 mV, Z<sub>1</sub> = 10 kΩ, Z<sub>2</sub> = 50 kΩ and Z<sub>cm</sub> = 100 MΩ:
answer.pre:
V<sub>d</sub>(false) = V<sub>cm</sub> × [Z<sub>cm</sub>/(Z<sub>cm</sub> + Z<sub>1</sub>) − Z<sub>cm</sub>/(Z<sub>cm</sub> + Z<sub>2</sub>)]
         ≈ V<sub>cm</sub> × (Z<sub>2</sub> − Z<sub>1</sub>) / Z<sub>cm</sub>
         = 100 mV × 40 kΩ / 100 MΩ = 40 µV

answer: A false 40 µV differential signal is as large as an EEG, and no CMRR can remove it because it is already differential at the input. So the impedances must be low and equal, and Z<sub>cm</sub> must be very high.

Rule of thumb. To lose less than 1 %, Z<sub>in</sub> ≥ 100 × Z<sub>e</sub>: 5 MΩ for a 50 kΩ surface contact, 1 GΩ for a 10 MΩ microelectrode. Modern instrumentation amplifiers offer 10⁹ Ω or more, and a driven right leg lowers V<sub>cm</sub> itself.
Closing check: 1 MΩ input with 50 kΩ electrode passes 95.2 %; a 40 kΩ mismatch on 100 mV common-mode through 100 MΩ gives 40 µV of false signal.

bank.q: Compare surface, needle and microelectrodes with respect to size, impedance, signal amplitude and clinical use.
outline: Surface: large area, lowest impedance (1–10 kΩ with gel and skin preparation), non-invasive, used for ECG, EEG and surface EMG
Needle: penetrates the skin, small exposed tip so higher impedance than a gelled surface electrode, used for needle EMG and the foetal scalp ECG
Microelectrode: tip 1 µm or less, impedance 1–100 MΩ, used for single-cell recording
Table of size, impedance, bandwidth and typical signal range
Sterilisation, safety and disposable versus reusable practice
answer: Purpose. All three convert ionic current to electronic current, but they differ in how close they get to the source and therefore in size, impedance and the signal they see.

head: Property
Surface
Needle
Microelectrode
rows: tip or bare core well under 1 mm
about 1–10 kΩ with gel and skin preparation
higher, because the exposed area is small
summed activity: ECG about 1 mV, EEG 10–100 µV, surface EMG 0.1–5 mV
single motor units, up to a few mV
one cell: intracellular the full −70 mV rest and 100 mV spike
yes, into or beside a cell

answer: Surface types. Plate or disc (Ag/AgCl on foam with gel, disposable), reusable plate held by a strap, suction cup for limb leads, and floating electrodes whose metal is recessed behind a gel column so that movement does not disturb the double layer.

Needle types. A monopolar needle is insulated except at the tip and used against a surface reference, so it sees a wide region. A concentric needle carries a fine wire inside a cannula; wire and cannula are the two poles, so the pickup volume is small and single motor unit potentials can be read.

Microelectrode types. A glass micropipette is pulled to a fine tip and filled with 3 M KCl; a metal microelectrode is tungsten or platinum–iridium etched to a point. The high tip resistance with the cable capacitance forms a low-pass filter, so the first amplifier stage sits close to the electrode.

Safety and handling. Surface electrodes are usually disposable; needles are sterile single-use; any electrode is a path into the body, so leakage current limits apply, strictest for intracardiac electrodes.
Closing check: a 10 MΩ glass tip on a 1 GΩ amplifier passes 1 ÷ 1.01 = 99.0 % of the signal; the same tip on a 1 MΩ ECG input would pass only 1 ÷ 11 = 9 %.

bank.q: List the criteria for selecting a physiological transducer and apply them to a blood-pressure sensor and a foot-pressure sensor.
outline: Range, sensitivity, linearity, hysteresis, resolution, bandwidth
Impedance matching, excitation requirement, output type
Biocompatibility, sterilisation, size, weight, safety, cost
Resistive strain-gauge type for blood pressure via diaphragm
Piezoelectric or resistive pressure pad for pedobarograph
Reasoned comparison against capacitive and inductive alternatives

head: Criterion
Meaning
rows: span of input over which the stated accuracy holds; overload limit above it
difference between rising and falling readings
bandwidth wide enough for the fastest part of the signal
what supply it needs and what it gives (mV, charge, current)
how much it disturbs the body
safe, sterile or cleanable, small, light

answer: Blood-pressure sensor (invasive, through a fluid-filled catheter). Range about −50 to +300 mmHg; a resistive strain-gauge (piezoresistive) diaphragm in a full bridge suits it because it reads steady as well as changing pressure.

answer.text: Working numbers for the BP sensor. A standard disposable transducer gives 5 µV per volt of excitation per mmHg:
answer.pre:
sensitivity at 5 V excitation = 5 µV/V/mmHg × 5 V = 25 µV/mmHg
output at 120 mmHg = 25 µV × 120 = 3.0 mV
output at 300 mmHg = 25 µV × 300 = 7.5 mV

answer: Bandwidth for BP: at 120 beats/min the pulse fundamental is 2 Hz, and the waveform needs about ten harmonics, so the sensor and catheter must be flat to about 20 Hz. It must be sterile, disposable and electrically isolated because the fluid column connects to the heart.

Foot-pressure sensor (pedobarograph). Needs many small cells, so each is a thin resistive or capacitive pad about 5 mm across. Range: normal peak pressures are a few hundred kPa and diabetic hot spots go higher. Hysteresis and creep matter more than raw sensitivity because loading rises and falls every step.

answer.text: Working numbers for a 5 mm cell:
answer.pre:
cell area = 5 mm × 5 mm = 25 × 10⁻⁶ m²
12.5 N on one cell → P = 12.5 / 25 × 10⁻⁶ = 500 kPa

answer: Why not other families. A piezoelectric pad gives charge only while force changes, so it cannot hold a standing pressure and is unsuitable for the pedobarograph or for mean BP. Capacitive cells are a good alternative for the foot (thin, sensitive) but need careful shielding; inductive (LVDT) sensors are too bulky for both.
Closing check: 120 mmHg gives 3.0 mV at 5 V excitation; one 5 mm cell at 12.5 N reads 500 kPa.

svg.aria: Block diagram of an ECG recorder: electrodes, lead selector with protection, buffer and instrumentation amplifier, filters, isolation and gain, ADC, and display, with a 1 millivolt calibration pulse injected at the input.

answer: Electrodes and lead selector. Ag/AgCl electrodes on RA, LA, LL, RL and V1–V6. The lead selector (now a resistor network or software) forms I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF and V1–V6. Protection diodes and series resistors guard the input against defibrillator pulses.

Buffer and instrumentation amplifier. Input impedance above 10 MΩ (10⁹ Ω in modern parts), first-stage gain kept low, about 10, so a 300 mV electrode offset gives only 3 V and cannot saturate. CMRR 100 dB or more, helped by a driven right leg.

Filters. High-pass 0.05 Hz for diagnostic recording (0.5 Hz for monitoring) removes offset and baseline wander; low-pass 150 Hz (40 Hz for monitors) removes muscle noise and acts as the anti-alias filter; a 50 Hz notch removes residual hum.

Isolation, gain and ADC. An isolation barrier keeps patient leakage below about 10 µA; the second stage brings the total gain to about 1000 so 1 mV becomes 1 V; a 12-bit ADC at 500 samples/s digitises it.

Display and calibration. Standard sensitivity 10 mm/mV and paper speed 25 mm/s, so one small square is 0.04 s and 0.1 mV. The 1 mV calibration pulse must draw a 10 mm bar on every channel before any reading is trusted.

head: Wave
Meaning
Duration
Amplitude
rows: about 1 mV (1–2 mV in chest leads)

answer: Leads. I = LA − RA, II = LL − RA, III = LL − LA (Einthoven's law II = I + III); aVR, aVL and aVF are augmented unipolar leads; V1–V6 are measured against the Wilson central terminal.

answer.pre:
RR = 20 mm at 25 mm/s → 20 / 25 = 0.80 s → HR = 60 / 0.80 = 75 bpm
R wave 12 mm at 10 mm/mV → 1.2 mV
QRS 2 mm wide → 2 / 25 = 0.08 s (normal)

answer: Closing check: 1 mV × total gain 1000 = 1 V at the ADC; leakage below 10 µA; 75 bpm and 0.08 s QRS are normal values.

bank.q: A bio-amplifier must handle a 1 mV differential ECG signal sitting on a 300 mV common-mode interference. Explain how an instrumentation amplifier solves this and calculate the CMRR needed if the interference at the output must stay at or below 0.1% of the signal.
outline: Differential gain A<sub>d</sub> and common-mode gain A<sub>cm</sub> defined
Instrumentation amplifier built from three op-amps; input buffers give very high impedance
CMRR = 20 log₁₀(A<sub>d</sub>/A<sub>cm</sub>)
Interference at the output A<sub>cm</sub> × 300 mV must be at most 10⁻³ × A<sub>d</sub> × 1 mV, so A<sub>d</sub>/A<sub>cm</sub> must be at least 3 × 10⁵
CMRR at least 20 log₁₀(3 × 10⁵) = 109.5 dB; a driven right leg that lowers the common-mode voltage relaxes this
Shielded cable, driven right leg and notch filter as supporting measures
answer: Definitions. Differential input V<sub>d</sub> = V<sub>1</sub> − V<sub>2</sub>; common-mode input V<sub>cm</sub> = (V<sub>1</sub> + V<sub>2</sub>) ÷ 2. Differential gain A<sub>d</sub>, common-mode gain A<sub>cm</sub>; CMRR = A<sub>d</sub> ÷ A<sub>cm</sub>, in dB 20 log₁₀(A<sub>d</sub> ÷ A<sub>cm</sub>).
The problem. Here V<sub>d</sub> = 1 mV and V<sub>cm</sub> = 300 mV: the interference is 300 times the signal at the input, so a single-ended amplifier would show mostly mains.

Instrumentation amplifier. Two input buffers (op-amps A1, A2) sense the electrodes with input impedance above 10⁹ Ω and give differential gain G = 1 + 2R/R<sub>g</sub> while passing the common-mode voltage at unity gain. A third op-amp, a difference amplifier with laser-trimmed resistors, subtracts the two buffer outputs and removes the common-mode part. The single resistor R<sub>g</sub> sets the gain without upsetting the balance.

answer.text: Required CMRR. The output interference must be at most 0.1 % of the output signal:
answer.pre:
A<sub>cm</sub> × 300 mV ≤ 0.001 × A<sub>d</sub> × 1 mV
A<sub>d</sub> / A<sub>cm</sub> ≥ 300 / 0.001 = 3 × 10⁵
CMRR ≥ 20 log₁₀(3 × 10⁵) = 109.5 dB

A<sub>cm</sub> = 1000 / (3 × 10⁵) = 3.33 × 10⁻³
signal out       = 1000 × 1 mV = 1 V
interference out = 3.33 × 10⁻³ × 300 mV = 1.0 mV = 0.1 % of 1 V

answer: Gain distribution. Electrode offset of up to 300 mV is differential DC, so the first stage gain must stay low: with G = 10, 300 mV becomes 3 V, well inside a ±12 V supply. With R = 25 kΩ, R<sub>g</sub> = 2R ÷ (G − 1) = 50 kΩ ÷ 9 = 5.56 kΩ. A 0.05 Hz high-pass then removes the offset and a second stage adds gain 100, giving 1000 overall.

head: Measure
Effect
rows: feeds back the inverted common-mode voltage; if it lowers V<sub>cm</sub> from 300 mV to 10 mV, the CMRR needed falls to 10 mV ÷ (0.001 × 1 mV) = 10⁴ = 80 dB
less mains pick-up to begin with
removes what is left, at the cost of some ringing

answer: Closing check: 109.5 dB is above what a plain op-amp difference stage gives (about 50 dB with 0.1 % resistors) and within reach of a good instrumentation amplifier (100–120 dB), so the INA with a driven right leg meets the 0.1 % target.

bank.q: A load cell has four strain gauges of 350 Ω and gauge factor 2.0, all four active in a Wheatstone bridge fed with 5 V. Strain is 1000 µε. Compute the output voltage and explain how this becomes a patient weight.
outline: Gauge factor definition G = (ΔR/R)/(ΔL/L)
Fractional resistance change = 2.0 × 1000 × 10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10⁻³
All-four-active bridge output ≈ V × (ΔR/R), giving about 10 mV
Amplify to a few volts, digitise with the ADC
Calibration with known weights; zeroing before each use
Load cell used in weighing scales and in gait platforms
answer: Gauge factor. GF = (ΔR ÷ R) ÷ ε, so ΔR ÷ R = GF × ε = 2.0 × 1000 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.0 × 10⁻³, and ΔR = 350 Ω × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 0.70 Ω.

Bridge arrangement. In a full bridge two gauges are in tension (R + ΔR) and two in compression (R − ΔR), placed so their effects add. Then the output is exactly V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>ex</sub> × ΔR ÷ R, four times the quarter-bridge value.

answer.pre:
V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>ex</sub> × GF × ε = 5 V × 2.0 × 1 × 10⁻³ = 10 mV
quarter bridge for comparison: 10 mV / 4 = 2.5 mV

answer: Rated output. If 1000 µε is the strain at the cell's 200 kg capacity, the rated output is 10 mV ÷ 5 V = 2 mV/V. The output is proportional to load, so it scales with excitation and with weight.

answer.text: From millivolts to a patient weight (75 kg patient):

answer: Calibration. Zero (tare) with nothing on the platform, then apply a known mass, for example 50 kg, and store the counts-per-kilogram slope; check at a second mass for linearity. A bed scale sums four cells, one under each leg, so the weight does not depend on where the patient lies.

Error sources and cures: temperature changes the gauge resistance (the full bridge cancels most of it because all four arms change together); creep and hysteresis of the spring element; lead resistance (six-wire sense connection).
Uses: patient and bed scales, infusion and dialysis fluid weighing, and force platforms in gait laboratories.
Closing check: full bridge 10 mV is 4 × the 2.5 mV quarter-bridge value; 75 kg reads 1228 counts at about 61 g per count.

bank.q: In a nerve conduction study the median nerve is stimulated at the wrist and at the elbow. Latency is 3.5 ms at the wrist and 7.5 ms at the elbow, and the separation is 240 mm. Calculate the conduction velocity and state how the result is interpreted.
outline: Latency difference = 7.5 − 3.5 = 4.0 ms, which removes the distal motor delay
Distance = 0.24 m
Compare with the normal value for the arm, about 50 m/s or more
Slowing suggests demyelination; small amplitude suggests axonal loss
Temperature and limb position affect the value
answer: Set-up. Recording electrodes over the abductor pollicis brevis (active over the belly, reference over the tendon), ground electrode between stimulating and recording sites. A constant-current stimulator gives 0.1–0.2 ms pulses; the current is raised until the CMAP stops growing and then increased a further 20 % or so (supramaximal), so all fibres fire.

Distal and proximal latencies. Stimulus at the wrist: onset latency 3.5 ms. Stimulus at the elbow: onset latency 7.5 ms. Both include the same fixed delay: conduction in the terminal branches, the neuromuscular junction and muscle activation.

answer.pre:
Δt = t<sub>proximal</sub> − t<sub>distal</sub> = 7.5 − 3.5 = 4.0 ms
d  = 240 mm = 0.240 m
v  = d / Δt = 240 mm / 4.0 ms = 60 mm/ms = 60 m/s
SI check: 0.240 m / 0.0040 s = 60 m/s

answer: Why subtract. Using the elbow latency alone would give 240 ÷ 7.5 = 32 m/s, falsely slow, because the distal delay would be counted as nerve conduction.

head: Finding
Suggests
rows: v about 50 m/s or more in the forearm, normal amplitude
v clearly slow (for example 35 m/s), amplitude kept
distal latency long, forearm v normal
slowing at the wrist, as in carpal tunnel syndrome

answer: Sources of error. Distance: ±10 mm on 240 mm gives 230 ÷ 4.0 = 57.5 to 250 ÷ 4.0 = 62.5 m/s, a ±4 % spread; measure along the nerve with the elbow at the same angle for both stimuli. Temperature: a cool limb conducts slowly, roughly 1.5–2.5 m/s per degree, so keep the skin warm and record its temperature. Latency cursor placement at the onset, not the peak.
Closing check: Δt = 4.0 ms, v = 60 m/s, within the normal range for the median motor nerve in the forearm.

bank.q: Design the recording chain for an EMG channel and for an EEG channel, stating gain, bandwidth, filter and sampling rate for each, and justify the differences.
outline: EEG amplitude 10–100 µV, band 0.5–70 Hz, gain of order 10⁴–10⁵
EMG amplitude 0.1–5 mV, band 10–500 Hz, gain of order 10²–10³
High-pass removes electrode drift; low-pass suppresses muscle noise in EEG
Notch at 50 Hz for mains interference
Sampling above twice the highest frequency: 250 Hz for EEG, 1–2 kHz for EMG
Common-mode rejection and input impedance requirements common to both

head: Item
EEG channel
EMG channel (surface)
rows: Ag/AgCl cups on the 10–20 sites, impedance below 5 kΩ
Ag/AgCl discs over muscle belly and tendon

answer: Front end common to both. Instrumentation amplifier with input impedance of 10⁹ Ω or more, CMRR of 100 dB or more, low first-stage gain (about 10) so electrode offset cannot saturate it, a driven right leg, and an isolation barrier for patient safety.

Why the gains differ. EMG is typically 20–50 times larger than EEG. EEG gain 10⁴ applied to a 2 mV EMG would give 20 V and clip; EMG gain 500 applied to a 50 µV EEG would give only 25 mV, a small part of the ADC range with poor resolution.

Why the bands differ. EEG rhythms (delta to beta) lie below 30 Hz with useful content to about 70 Hz; anything above is mostly muscle, so the EEG low-pass removes it. MUAPs have fast edges, so EMG needs content up to about 500 Hz; its 20 Hz high-pass removes movement artefact that would swamp a surface EMG.

Why the sampling rates differ. The rate must exceed twice the top of the band with margin: 250 > 2 × 70 = 140 samples/s for EEG; 2000 > 2 × 500 = 1000 samples/s for EMG. The analog low-pass must come first, because aliased noise cannot be removed afterwards.

answer.pre:
EEG, 21 channels: 21 × 250 × 2 = 10.5 kB/s → 18.9 MB for 30 minutes
EMG, 2 channels:   2 × 2000 × 2 = 8 kB/s

answer: EMG processing after the ADC: rectify, then mean absolute value or RMS over a window (for example 0.70 mV and 0.775 mV for the samples 0.4, −0.8, 1.2, −0.4 mV), and the median frequency for fatigue.
Closing check: both outputs sit near 0.5–1 V at the ADC; both Nyquist frequencies (125 Hz and 1000 Hz) lie above their bands.

bank.q: Explain how a heart-rate monitor detects beats, and how a Holter monitor differs from it in recording, leads and analysis.
outline: QRS detection by amplitude threshold or slope/derivative algorithm
Beat-to-beat interval, averaging over 8–10 beats, bradycardia and tachycardia alarms
Artefact rejection: T waves, muscle noise, motion
Holter: 2–3 modified chest leads, 24 hours, solid-state memory
Scanning for ST episodes, arrhythmias, heart-rate variability, patient diary
Maintenance points for both: battery, electrodes, calibration
answer: Heart-rate monitor chain. Electrodes and ECG amplifier, then a band-pass filter of about 5–15 Hz (the QRS band), which removes P and T waves, baseline wander and high-frequency noise.

Beat detection. The filtered signal is differentiated (QRS edges are the steepest part of the ECG), squared or rectified, and compared with an adaptive threshold. After each detection a refractory window of about 200 ms blocks a second count from the same QRS or a tall T wave.

answer.pre:
instantaneous HR = 60 / RR, e.g. RR = 0.80 s → 75 bpm
average over 8 beats: RR = 0.80, 0.82, 0.78, 0.80, 0.79, 0.81, 0.80, 0.80 s
mean RR = 6.40 / 8 = 0.80 s → 75 bpm

answer: Display and alarms. The averaged value is shown because it is steady; the beat-to-beat value drives trends. Alarms sound below the low limit (bradycardia, for example 50 bpm) or above the high limit (tachycardia, for example 120 bpm) set by the clinician.

Holter recorder. A small battery recorder worn for 24–48 h with two or three modified chest leads. Every sample is stored with a time stamp, formerly on cassette, now on flash memory. A three-channel record at 250 samples/s in 1.5-byte samples needs 3 × 250 × 86,400 × 1.5 = 97.2 MB per day.

Holter analysis. Replay software detects every QRS, classifies beats, trends heart rate, counts pauses and ectopic beats, looks for ST episodes and heart-rate variability, and links events to the patient diary and event button. The average rate is total beats ÷ total minutes, for example 108,000 ÷ 1440 = 75 bpm.

head: Item
Heart-rate monitor
Holter
rows: live rate and alarms at the bedside

answer: Maintenance for both: fresh electrodes and gel, check the cable and lead-off detection, check the battery and the clock, and confirm the 1 mV calibration.
Closing check: 60 ÷ 0.80 s = 75 bpm and 108,000 ÷ 1440 min = 75 bpm agree; 97.2 MB per day fits many days on a 1 GB card.

bank.q: An ECG recording shows a thick 50 Hz baseline. Separate the possible faults into patient, electrode, amplifier and interference categories, and give the check and the cure for each.
outline: Patient: movement, sweating, shivering — rest and reassure
Electrode: dry or loose, old jelly, high impedance, wrong half-cell metal — clean skin, new Ag/AgCl electrodes
Amplifier: gain, filter, calibration and lead-off settings — check calibration pulse
Interference: broken shield, ungrounded bed, mains and diathermy nearby — use driven right leg, notch filter, shielded cable
Wandering baseline from respiration and electrode drift
Decide by substitution: swap cable, swap electrodes, use simulator
answer: Start with the raw trace. A thick 50 Hz band on every lead points to the common path (ground, driven right leg, mains environment); a band on one lead points to that electrode or lead wire. A clean QRS shape under the fuzz shows the amplifier itself works.

head: Category
Possible fault
Check
Cure
rows: touching a metal bed rail or the mains-powered bed; shivering or tense muscles (gives fast irregular fuzz, not a pure 50 Hz)
look at the patient and the bed
move hands away, warm and relax the patient
dry or old gel, loose electrode, unprepared skin, mixed electrode types
impedance check; does wiping and reapplying one electrode clear it?
abrade skin, fresh Ag/AgCl electrodes of one type
broken lead shield, open right-leg lead, faulty input stage, notch switched off
swap the patient cable; run the patient simulator
replace cable; service the input stage; switch the notch on
nearby mains cables, lamps, other equipment, unearthed bed, diathermy
switch off nearby equipment one by one
reroute leads away from mains, earth the bed, use shielded twisted leads

answer.text: Why unequal electrodes matter so much. With 100 mV common-mode on the body, electrode impedances of 10 kΩ and 50 kΩ and an amplifier common-mode impedance of 100 MΩ:
answer.pre: false differential = 100 mV × (50 − 10) kΩ / 100 MΩ = 40 µV of 50 Hz

answer: That 40 µV is already differential, so even a perfect CMRR passes it; only matched, low-impedance electrodes cure it.

answer.text: Why CMRR and the driven right leg matter. With a gain of 1000 and CMRR of 80 dB (10⁴):
answer.pre:
A<sub>cm</sub> = 1000 / 10⁴ = 0.1
100 mV common-mode → 0.1 × 100 mV = 10 mV of hum on a 1 V ECG (1 %)
a driven right leg lowering V<sub>cm</sub> to 10 mV → 1 mV of hum (0.1 %)

answer: Not to be confused with 50 Hz: baseline wander (slow swing from breathing or sweat, fixed by skin preparation and the 0.05–0.5 Hz high-pass) and muscle artefact (irregular fast spikes, fixed by relaxing the patient).

Decide by substitution. Connect a patient simulator giving a clean 1 mV ECG: if the trace is clean, the fault is at the patient or electrodes; if the hum stays, swap the cable; if it still stays, the amplifier or the earth is at fault. Confirm the 10 mm calibration bar after the repair.

Closing check: 40 µV from a 40 kΩ mismatch is 4 % of a 1 mV ECG; a driven right leg that cuts V<sub>cm</sub> tenfold (20 dB), from 100 mV to 10 mV, cuts the CMRR-limited hum tenfold, from 10 mV to 1 mV.

bank.q: Discuss multichannel EEG recording in epilepsy, the use of evoked potentials, and the place of MEG as a complementary method.
outline: Electrode placement by the 10–20 system; 19 or 21 channels; montages
Epilepsy: interictal spikes and slow waves, focus localisation, activation procedures
Averaging for visual, auditory and somatosensory evoked potentials, 100–1000 trials
Latency and amplitude of the recovered waveform used in diagnosis
MEG measures the magnetic field of the same currents; needs shielding and SQUID sensors
Evaluate: EEG gives good temporal but poor spatial resolution; MEG better spatial, higher cost; combinations are complementary
answer: Electrode placement. The 10–20 system places 19 scalp electrodes (21 with the two ear references) at 10 % and 20 % steps of the nasion–inion and ear-to-ear distances: Fp, F, C, P, O and T sites, odd numbers left, even right, z midline. High-density caps use 64–256.

Multichannel amplifier. One channel per derivation, gain 10⁴–10⁵, CMRR above 80 dB, band 0.5–70 Hz, 50 Hz notch, sampled at 250 samples/s or more; display sensitivity about 7 µV/mm and paper speed 30 mm/s, so one 300 mm page shows 10 s.

Montages. Referential: each electrode against one reference (linked ears, average); shows the field at each site. Bipolar chains (Fp1–F3, F3–C3, ...): adjacent pairs; a focal spike shows as a phase reversal between two channels that share the electrode nearest the focus.

head: Pattern
Duration or rate
Meaning
rows: Focal spikes in a few channels
focal epilepsy; phase reversal locates the focus

answer: Recording practice for epilepsy. Interictal spikes between seizures help locate the focus; activation by hyperventilation (3 minutes), flashing light and sleep deprivation brings them out; ictal recording uses long-term video-EEG to capture an event.

Evoked potentials. A repeated stimulus gives a small response, about 1 µV, time-locked to it. VEP: reversing checkerboard, P100 near 100 ms over the occiput. BAEP: clicks, waves I–V within 10 ms. SSEP: median nerve pulses, N20 near 20 ms over the sensory cortex.

answer.text: Averaging. The response repeats with fixed latency; the background EEG is random with respect to the stimulus, so averaging N trials raises the SNR by √N:
answer.pre:
EP 1 µV, background 2 µV → SNR₁ = 0.5
wanted SNR 10 → √N = 10 / 0.5 = 20 → N = 400 trials

answer: Artefact rejection drops trials with blinks or movement before averaging, because a large artefact locked to the stimulus would survive the average.

MEG. The same cortical currents make a magnetic field of about 10–1000 fT. The Earth's field is about 50 µT = 5 × 10¹⁰ fT, some 10⁸ times larger, so MEG needs a magnetically shielded room and SQUID sensors cooled by liquid helium, arranged in a helmet of 100–300 channels.

Conclusion. EEG is the first-line, low-cost tool for epilepsy and the base for evoked potentials; MEG complements it when the focus must be located precisely before surgery. Recorded together and placed on an MRI, they give both timing and place.
Closing check: 400 trials give SNR 0.5 × √400 = 10; a 300 mm EEG page at 30 mm/s is 10 s.

bank.q: Describe the instrumentation for EEG and EMG biofeedback and evaluate the factors that decide whether such training can succeed.
outline: Electrodes, high-gain low-noise amplifier, band-pass filter for the chosen band
Rectify and integrate, or count events, to get one slowly varying number
Feedback within a fraction of a second; visual bar or audio tone with threshold
Baseline session, threshold raised gradually, number of sessions
Evaluate: signal quality, latency, patient motivation, artefact from eye blinks and jaw clonus
Uses: relaxation training, re-education of pelvic-floor and wrist muscles
answer: Instrumentation chain. Surface electrodes (scalp for EEG, over the muscle for EMG), a low-noise instrumentation amplifier with high CMRR, a band-pass filter for the chosen band (alpha 8–13 Hz, or EMG 20–500 Hz) plus a 50 Hz notch, a full-wave rectifier, a smoother (low-pass, time constant about 0.1–1 s), a comparator with hysteresis, and a tone, light or bar display. The patient closes the loop.
Alternative displays. Instead of on/off, the envelope can drive a bar graph or a tone whose pitch rises with level, which gives graded information; event counters count alpha bursts per minute.
Training protocol. A baseline session measures the resting level; the threshold starts where the patient succeeds often, then moves gradually; sessions of 20–30 minutes are repeated over weeks.

head: Factor
Why it matters
rows: the tone must follow the body, not 50 Hz hum, blinks, jaw clenching or ECG pick-up
the smoother delays the envelope; keep the total under about half a second so action and tone are linked
success often enough to motivate, but not so often that the tone means nothing; when silence is the reward the rule reverses
stops chatter near threshold (on at 15 mV, off at 12 mV)
motivation, understanding of the link between effort and tone, number of sessions
isolated patient circuit and low leakage, even though nothing is stimulated

answer: Uses: relaxation and tension-headache training (frontalis EMG), muscle re-education after stroke or injury and pelvic-floor training (EMG), and alpha or attention training (EEG).

Evaluation. EMG biofeedback has the stronger signal (millivolts) and clearer link to a voluntary action, so it is easier to make work; EEG biofeedback needs microvolt-level clean signals and more sessions, and its benefits are less certain. Either way the machine only informs: the patient does the learning.
Closing check: 20 µV × 1000 = 20 mV; 0.90 × 20 mV = 18.0 mV is above 15 mV, and 10.8 mV is below 12 mV.

bank.q: For a gait laboratory, choose sensors for foot pressure, joint angle, velocity and acceleration, and explain how the numbers are combined to describe a walking cycle.
outline: Pedobarograph platform or insole for plantar pressure mapping
Potentiometer, goniometer or IMU for limb position and joint angle
Accelerometer and gyroscope for acceleration and angular velocity
Velocity from integration of acceleration or from timing markers
Walking cycle: heel strike, loading, stance, toe-off, swing
Evaluate: cable tangle versus wireless IMU, calibration, drift and repeatability

head: Quantity
Sensor
Why
rows: pedobarograph platform or insole (resistive or capacitive cells about 5 mm)
shows where load falls; insole records many steps
accurate total force and centre of pressure

answer.pre:
cell 5 mm × 5 mm = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²; 12.5 N → 500 kPa peak
480 loaded cells → 0.012 m²; 70 kg × 9.81 = 686.7 N → mean 57.2 kPa

answer: Gait cycle. From heel strike to the next heel strike of the same foot: loading response, mid-stance, terminal stance, pre-swing (toe-off), then swing. Stance is about 60 % and swing 40 % of the cycle in normal walking; the pressure insole marks heel strike and toe-off, so it gives the phase times directly.

answer.pre:
step length 0.7 m, cadence 120 steps/min = 2.0 steps/s
speed = 0.7 × 2.0 = 1.4 m/s; stride = 1.4 m; cycle = 1.0 s
stance = 0.60 × 1.0 = 0.60 s; swing = 0.40 s

answer.text: Velocity from markers, and the IMU route:
answer.pre:
heel marker moves 0.028 m in one 0.02 s frame (50 frames/s)
v = Δx / Δt = 0.028 / 0.02 = 1.4 m/s (agrees with the walk)
IMU: a<sub>motion</sub> = a<sub>measured</sub> − g<sub>axis</sub>, then integrate once for v and twice for x

answer.text: Why the IMU drifts. Even after gravity is removed, a small bias b integrates:
answer.pre:
b = 0.05 m/s² → velocity error b t = 0.5 m/s after 10 s
position error ½ b t² = ½ × 0.05 × 10² = 2.5 m after 10 s

answer: So the IMU is reset at each foot-flat (when the foot is known to be still), and the camera system is kept as the laboratory reference.

Evaluation. Cameras are accurate and drift-free but fixed to the lab; IMUs and insoles are wireless and work outdoors but need calibration and drift control; goniometers are simple but strapping them across a joint can shift. Sample at about 100 samples/s, since gait detail lies below 10–20 Hz.
Closing check: 1.4 m/s from step length and cadence agrees with 1.4 m/s from the marker; stance 0.60 s plus swing 0.40 s equals the 1.0 s cycle.

glossary.def: Voltage produced by living tissue, such as the membrane voltage of a nerve or muscle cell or the body-surface copy of many such cells.
Loss of the negative resting voltage as positive ions enter the cell.
Return of the membrane voltage to its resting negative value after an action potential.
Short time after an action potential when the cell cannot fire again, which limits the maximum firing rate.
Active transport that pushes Na⁺ out and K⁺ in to keep the concentration gradients that make the resting potential.
Silver wire coated with silver chloride, used as a stable, low-offset, non-polarisable biopotential electrode.
Build-up of charge at an electrode that opposes current flow and distorts low-frequency signals.
False signal caused by movement of the electrode on the skin, which changes the half-cell potential.
Electrode pair that records the difference between two nearby active sites.
Active electrode referred to one distant common reference, so the signal contains more of the remote activity.
Electrode placed over the source of interest; the other is the reference or indifferent electrode.
Ratio of fractional resistance change to fractional length change in a strain gauge, about 2 for metal foil.
Force transducer made of a metal element with bonded strain gauges wired as a Wheatstone bridge.
Sensor that converts displacement or pressure into a change of capacitance.
Sensor that converts displacement into a change of inductance, for example by moving a core in a coil.
Sensor that converts light intensity into current or voltage, used for pulse and blood-oxygen measurement.
Circuit that passes the signal across an optical or transformer barrier so no mains fault current can reach the patient.
Narrow band-stop filter, usually set at 50 Hz in India, that removes mains interference with little loss elsewhere.
Analogue-to-digital converter; its resolution in bits and its sampling rate set the quality of the stored signal.
False low-frequency signal created when the sampling rate is below twice the highest signal frequency.
Time from a stimulus to the start of the evoked or muscle response, measured in milliseconds.
Fall in the median frequency and rise in amplitude of the EMG spectrum as a muscle is held contracted.
Standard spacing of EEG electrodes by percentages of the skull landmarks, giving named positions such as Fz, C3 and O2.
Superconducting quantum interference device, the extremely sensitive magnetic sensor used in MEG.
